newsitem.title: USA: US aluminum/zinc premiums firm despite slow trade.
newsitem.headline: US aluminum/zinc premiums firm despite slow trade.

text.p: Aluminum and zinc physical markets in the United States remain fairly buoyant with slight gains in premiums noted despite the sluggish holiday atmosphere permeating much of the metals industry.
Although premiums were showing signs of creeping higher, the volume of business was not especially heavy with many traders away from their desks due to the year-end holidays.
Aluminum premiums were making further gains, with traders quoting 4.75 cents per pound over LME cash as a new floor with the upper end of the range at 5.00 to 5.25 cents.
"Everyone is a buyer. There is good producer and trader buying," one dealer said.
Deals for delivery in the first quarter of 1997 were being settled at or just below 5 cents per pound, traders said.
Further gains in premiums were inevitable before metal was imported from Europe or obtained from other sources to put dowside pressure on the market, traders added.

Firmer LME aluminum prices have also kept U.S. scrap prices on a firming trend, along with physical alloy tags which are consolidating their recent climb to 70 to 71 cents per pound for delivered A380 grade metal in the Midwest.
"The scrap market is tightening up a little bit," a smelter official said. "Alloy business seems to be pretty good for the first quarter."
Zinc metal premiums also remain healthy at a solid 5.50 to 6.00 cents per pound over LME cash, trader and producer agents said.
Zinc premiums were said to be particularly strong in the Midwest now the big Great Lakes freeze was starting.
"I think premiums are going to hold or even creep up in the next two to three weeks," a dealer said.

Although the usual steps were taken to stock up on metal in the Midwest before the freeze up, demand has been so steady that not much metal was left and premiums will have rise to attract more material at higher freight costs from locations such as Baltimore and elsewhere on the east coast, the dealer added.
"Business is very good and supply is tight," a producer linked trader said.

The slump in LME nickel prices to their lowest levels in more than two years earlier this week failed, however, to stir much physical interest on the U.S. market, leaving premiums at their pre-holiday levels of 8 to 11 cents per pound over LME cash.
"We have had no inquiries at all, and I don't think there will be any change until the first week after New Year," a trader said. "All the buying for delivery next week has been done."
